claim: Movement restraint significantly reduced the hourly distance swam by 6 and 8 dpf in non-repeated experimental designs compared to unrestrained controls.
source: Movement restraint significantly reduced the hourly distance swam by 6 and 8 dpf in both non-repeated (Figure 1B; Treatment x Age Interaction: 1F2,80 = 14.08, p<0.01) and repeated (Figure 1C; Video 1; Treatment x Age Interaction: 2F2,34 = 14.16, p<0.01) experimental designs compared to unrestrained controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test with p<0.01) and reference to Figure 1B showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint significantly reduced the hourly distance swam by 6 and 8 dpf in repeated experimental designs compared to unrestrained controls.
source: Movement restraint significantly reduced the hourly distance swam by 6 and 8 dpf in both non-repeated (Figure 1B; Treatment x Age Interaction: 1F2,80 = 14.08, p<0.01) and repeated (Figure 1C; Video 1; Treatment x Age Interaction: 2F2,34 = 14.16, p<0.01) experimental designs compared to unrestrained controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test with p<0.01) and reference to Figure 1C and Video 1 showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint prevented the increase in the proportion of fast swims (>10 mm/s) first exhibited by control larvae on 6 dpf.
source: Furthermore, movement restraint also prevented the increase in the proportion of fast swims (>10 mm/s) first exhibited by control larvae on 6 dpf (Figure 1D–E; Treatment x Age Interaction: 3F2,68 = 14.90, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test with p<0.01) and reference to Figures 1D-E showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint did not affect larval body length by 6 dpf.
source: We found that movement restraint did not affect larval body length by 6 dpf, but reduced body length by 9 dpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; 4F2,111 = 13.10, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint reduced body length by 9 dpf.
source: We found that movement restraint did not affect larval body length by 6 dpf, but reduced body length by 9 dpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; 4F2,111 = 13.10, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test with p<0.01) and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing experimental data.

claim: Prior movement restraint did not impair hourly distance swam in unrestrained conditions.
source: Prior movement restraint did not impair either hourly distance swam (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; 5t20 = 0.98, p=0.34) or proportion of fast swims (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, 6t20 = 0.16, p=0.87) in unrestrained conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.34) and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing experimental data.

claim: Prior movement restraint did not impair proportion of fast swims in unrestrained conditions.
source: Prior movement restraint did not impair either hourly distance swam (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; 5t20 = 0.98, p=0.34) or proportion of fast swims (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, 6t20 = 0.16, p=0.87) in unrestrained conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.87) and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint significantly reduced the proportion of proliferative (PCNA+) cells in the forebrain of zebrafish by 6 dpf.
source: Movement restraint significantly reduced the proportion of proliferative (PCNA+) cells in the forebrain of zebrafish by 6 dpf (Figure 2A–C; 7t9 = 4.07, p<0.01) sampled across consecutive coronal sections (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), without affecting forebrain size (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.01) and reference to Figures 2A-C showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint did not affect forebrain size by 6 dpf.
source: Movement restraint significantly reduced the proportion of proliferative (PCNA+) cells in the forebrain of zebrafish by 6 dpf (Figure 2A–C; 7t9 = 4.07, p<0.01) sampled across consecutive coronal sections (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), without affecting forebrain size (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 2 showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint reduced the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the subpallium by 6 dpf.
source: This difference was attributed to a reduction in the proportion of PCNA+ cells in both the subpallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A; 8t5 = 3.77, p=0.01) and pallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B; 9t5 = 7.36, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.01) and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2A showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint reduced the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the pallium by 6 dpf.
source: This difference was attributed to a reduction in the proportion of PCNA+ cells in both the subpallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A; 8t5 = 3.77, p=0.01) and pallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B; 9t5 = 7.36, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.01) and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2B showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint did not affect the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the olfactory bulb by 6 dpf.
source: Conversely, movement restraint did not affect the size (Table 2) or proportion of PCNA+ cells in the olfactory bulb (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; 10t9 = 0.53, p=0.61) or optic tectum (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D; 11t8 = 0.87, p=0.41) by 6 dpf.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.61) and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2C showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint did not affect the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the optic tectum by 6 dpf.
source: Conversely, movement restraint did not affect the size (Table 2) or proportion of PCNA+ cells in the olfactory bulb (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; 10t9 = 0.53, p=0.61) or optic tectum (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D; 11t8 = 0.87, p=0.41) by 6 dpf.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.41) and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2D showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint reduced forebrain size by 9 dpf.
source: Movement restraint reduced forebrain size by 9 dpf (Table 2); however, after correcting for forebrain size, chronic restraint still significantly reduced the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the forebrain by 9 dpf compared to controls (Figure 2D–F; 12U = 0, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 2 showing experimental data.

claim: After correcting for forebrain size, chronic restraint significantly reduced the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the forebrain by 9 dpf compared to controls.
source: Movement restraint reduced forebrain size by 9 dpf (Table 2); however, after correcting for forebrain size, chronic restraint still significantly reduced the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the forebrain by 9 dpf compared to controls (Figure 2D–F; 12U = 0, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test with p<0.01) and reference to Figures 2D-F showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint reduced the proportion of tbr2+ cells in the pallium by 9 dpf.
source: Movement restraint also reduced the proportion of tbr2+ cells, a protein marker of intermediate progenitors and newly generated neurons (Englund et al., 2005), in the pallium by 9 dpf (Figure 2G–I; 13t16 = 3.37, p<0.01) without affecting the proportion of pallial GFAP+ radial neural stem cells in Tg(GFAP:gfp) embryos (Figure 2J–L; 14t12 = 0.35, p=0.73).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.01), reference to Figures 2G-I showing experimental data, and citation to Englund et al., 2005 for tbr2 marker characterization.

claim: Movement restraint did not affect the proportion of pallial GFAP+ radial neural stem cells in Tg(GFAP:gfp) embryos by 9 dpf.
source: Movement restraint also reduced the proportion of tbr2+ cells, a protein marker of intermediate progenitors and newly generated neurons (Englund et al., 2005), in the pallium by 9 dpf (Figure 2G–I; 13t16 = 3.37, p<0.01) without affecting the proportion of pallial GFAP+ radial neural stem cells in Tg(GFAP:gfp) embryos (Figure 2J–L; 14t12 = 0.35, p=0.73).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.73) and reference to Figures 2J-L showing experimental data.

claim: tbr2 is a protein marker of intermediate progenitors and newly generated neurons.
source: Movement restraint also reduced the proportion of tbr2+ cells, a protein marker of intermediate progenitors and newly generated neurons (Englund et al., 2005), in the pallium by 9 dpf (Figure 2G–I; 13t16 = 3.37, p<0.01) without affecting the proportion of pallial GFAP+ radial neural stem cells in Tg(GFAP:gfp) embryos (Figure 2J–L; 14t12 = 0.35, p=0.73).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Englund et al., 2005.

claim: Movement restraint significantly increased the proportion of newly generated cells that co-label with Elavl3 in the pallium.
source: Movement restraint significantly increased the proportion of newly generated cells that co-label with Elavl3 in both the pallium (Figure 2M; 15t6 = 6.02, p<0.01) and subpallium (Figure 2N–T; 16t6 = 3.43, p=0.01) without affecting the absolute number of EdU+ cells produced in the pallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E; 17t6 = 0.35, p=0.74) or subpallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F; 18t7 = 0.73, p=0.49).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.01) and reference to Figure 2M showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint significantly increased the proportion of newly generated cells that co-label with Elavl3 in the subpallium.
source: Movement restraint significantly increased the proportion of newly generated cells that co-label with Elavl3 in both the pallium (Figure 2M; 15t6 = 6.02, p<0.01) and subpallium (Figure 2N–T; 16t6 = 3.43, p=0.01) without affecting the absolute number of EdU+ cells produced in the pallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E; 17t6 = 0.35, p=0.74) or subpallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F; 18t7 = 0.73, p=0.49).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.01) and reference to Figures 2N-T showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint did not affect the absolute number of EdU+ cells produced in the pallium.
source: Movement restraint significantly increased the proportion of newly generated cells that co-label with Elavl3 in both the pallium (Figure 2M; 15t6 = 6.02, p<0.01) and subpallium (Figure 2N–T; 16t6 = 3.43, p=0.01) without affecting the absolute number of EdU+ cells produced in the pallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E; 17t6 = 0.35, p=0.74) or subpallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F; 18t7 = 0.73, p=0.49).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.74) and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2E showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint did not affect the absolute number of EdU+ cells produced in the subpallium.
source: Movement restraint significantly increased the proportion of newly generated cells that co-label with Elavl3 in both the pallium (Figure 2M; 15t6 = 6.02, p<0.01) and subpallium (Figure 2N–T; 16t6 = 3.43, p=0.01) without affecting the absolute number of EdU+ cells produced in the pallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E; 17t6 = 0.35, p=0.74) or subpallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F; 18t7 = 0.73, p=0.49).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.49) and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2F showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint did not affect the number of cells expressing activated caspase-3 in the forebrain by 6 dpf.
source: Conversely, movement restraint did not affect the number of cells expressing the apoptotic marker activated caspase-3 (Casp3) in the forebrain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G; 19t7 = 1.06, p=0.32) by 6 dpf.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.32) and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2G showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint significantly increased the number of activated Casp3+ cells in the forebrain by 9 dpf.
source: By 9 dpf, however, movement restraint significantly increased the number of activated Casp3+ cells in the forebrain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H; 20t13 = 3.56, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p<0.01) and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2H showing experimental data.

claim: The increase in apoptosis at 9 dpf was specific to the pallium.
source: This increase in apoptosis at 9 dpf was specific to the pallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I; 21U = 1, p<0.01) and not found in the subpallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2J; 22t13 = 1.76, p=0.10).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test with p<0.01) and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2I showing experimental data.

claim: The increase in apoptosis at 9 dpf was not found in the subpallium.
source: This increase in apoptosis at 9 dpf was specific to the pallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2I; 21U = 1, p<0.01) and not found in the subpallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2J; 22t13 = 1.76, p=0.10).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.10) and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2J showing experimental data.

claim: Larvae reared against a strong current exhibited a greater proportion of PCNA+ cells in the pallium on 9 dpf.
source: On 9 dpf, larvae reared against a strong current exhibited a greater proportion of PCNA+ cells in the pallium (Figure 3D; 25t15 = 2.80, p=0.01), but not the subpallium (Figure 3E; 26t19 = 1.22, p=0.24).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.01) and reference to Figure 3D showing experimental data.

claim: Larvae reared against a strong current did not exhibit a greater proportion of PCNA+ cells in the subpallium on 9 dpf.
source: On 9 dpf, larvae reared against a strong current exhibited a greater proportion of PCNA+ cells in the pallium (Figure 3D; 25t15 = 2.80, p=0.01), but not the subpallium (Figure 3E; 26t19 = 1.22, p=0.24).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.24) and reference to Figure 3E showing experimental data.

claim: The size of the pallium and subpallium was not affected by rearing treatment on 9 dpf.
source: On 9 dpf, the size of both brain regions was not affected by rearing treatment (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 2 showing experimental data.

claim: Larvae reared against a strong current exhibited an increase in the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the pallium at 6 dpf.
source: When we sampled pallial proliferation in larvae earlier, at 6 dpf, we again found an increase in the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the pallium in larvae reared against a strong current (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; 23t7 = 2.76, p=0.03), while the subpallium was unaffected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; 24t6 = 1.27, p=0.25).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.03) and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing experimental data.

claim: The subpallium was unaffected by rearing against a strong current at 6 dpf.
source: When we sampled pallial proliferation in larvae earlier, at 6 dpf, we again found an increase in the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the pallium in larvae reared against a strong current (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; 23t7 = 2.76, p=0.03), while the subpallium was unaffected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; 24t6 = 1.27, p=0.25).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.25) and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing experimental data.

claim: Rearing larvae against a current reduced the number of newly generated (EdU+) cells that also expressed Elavl3 compared to controls.
source: Rearing larvae against a current reduced the number of newly generated (EdU+) cells that also expressed Elavl3 compared to controls (Figure 3F; 27t11 = 2.39, p=0.04), consistent with increased movement maintaining an expanded proliferative cell population over the generation of differentiated neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.04) and reference to Figure 3F showing experimental data.

claim: Rearing larvae against a current from 3 to 9 dpf did not affect body length.
source: Rearing larvae against a current from 3 to 9 dpf did not affect body length (Figure 3G, 28U = 102, p=0.5081), suggesting these effects on pallial neurogenesis are not a product of overall growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U test with p=0.5081) and reference to Figure 3G showing experimental data.

claim: Blocking tail movement (complete immobilization) significantly reduced the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the pallium by 6 dpf.
source: Blocking tail movement (complete immobilization) significantly reduced the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the pallium by 6 dpf (Figure 4D; 29F2,14 = 7.89, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test with p<0.01) and reference to Figure 4D showing experimental data.

claim: Removing just visual stimulation had no impact on the number of PCNA+ cells in the pallium.
source: Conversely, removing just visual stimulation had no impact on the number of PCNA+ cells in the pallium.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental design described in the text and implied by the statistical results.

claim: Neither removing visual stimulation nor tail movement affected the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the subpallium.
source: Neither removing visual stimulation nor tail movement affected the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the subpallium (Figure 4E; 30F2,14 = 2.42, p=0.13).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test with p=0.13) and reference to Figure 4E showing experimental data.

claim: Immobilization did not reduce the total number of cells in the pallium or subpallium.
source: Immobilization did not reduce the total number of cells in the pallium or subpallium (Table 2), instead affecting the PCNA+ cell population specifically.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 2 showing experimental data.

claim: Copper sulfate treatment did not affect the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the 6 dpf larvae pallium when all larvae were reared in unrestrained wells.
source: However, copper sulfate treatment did not affect the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the 6 dpf larvae pallium (Figure 5B; 31t12 = 0.51, p=0.62) when all larvae were reared in unrestrained wells.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.62) and reference to Figure 5B showing experimental data.

claim: AG1478 treatment affected neither the pallium size nor proportion of pallial PCNA+ cells on 3 dpf, prior to any motor treatments.
source: However, AG1478 treatment affected neither the pallium size (Table 2) nor proportion of pallial PCNA+ cells on 3 dpf, prior to any motor treatments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; 32t7 = 0.04, p=0.97).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.97), reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1A showing experimental data, and reference to Table 2.

claim: Prior AG1478 treatment did not affect swimming compared to DMSO-treated controls by 6 dpf.
source: By 6 dpf, prior AG1478 treatment did not affect swimming compared to DMSO-treated controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B; 33F3,17 = 16.16, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test with p<0.01) and reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1B showing experimental data.

claim: Prior AG1478 treatment blocked the movement-dependent change in the proportion of pallial PCNA+ cells observed in DMSO-treated larvae.
source: Whereas DMSO-treated larvae exhibited a movement-dependent change in the proportion of pallial PCNA+ cells, prior AG1478 treatment blocked this effect (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C; 34F3,77 = 4.17, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test with p<0.01) and reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1C showing experimental data.

claim: Prior AG1478 treatment increased the number of newly generated (EdU+) cells that also express Elavl3 in unrestrained larvae exposed to EdU from 5 to 6 dpf.
source: Furthermore, when unrestrained larvae were exposed to EdU from 5 to 6 dpf as in our restraint paradigm, prior AG1478 treatment increased the number of newly generated (EdU+) cells that also express Elavl3 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D; 35t8 = 2.53, p=0.04) compared to DMSO-treated controls, suggesting early AG1478 treatment affects pallial neurogenesis similarly to chronic restraint, albeit at a reduced magnitude.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.04) and reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1D showing experimental data.

claim: Prior AG1478 treatment did not affect swimming on 8 dpf.
source: Prior AG1478 treatment also did not affect swimming on 8 dpf (Figure 6B; 36F3,20 = 27.59, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test with p<0.01) and reference to Figure 6B showing experimental data.

claim: By 9 dpf, AG1478-treated larvae exhibited movement-dependent differences in the proportion of pallial PCNA+ cells, however, the magnitude of this effect was significantly attenuated compared to DMSO-treated controls.
source: By 9 dpf, AG1478-treated larvae exhibited movement-dependent differences in the proportion of pallial PCNA+ cells, however, the magnitude of this effect was significantly attenuated compared to DMSO-treated controls (Figure 6C–G; 37F3,23 = 26.68, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test with p<0.01) and reference to Figures 6C-G showing experimental data.

claim: Unrestrained larval zebrafish incubated in Optovin exhibited intense, sporadic bouts of movement during light exposure.
source: Unrestrained larval zebrafish incubated in Optovin exhibited intense, sporadic bouts of movement during light exposure, presumably as spinal reflexes in response to intense DRG activation (Kokel et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation and citation to Kokel et al., 2013 for the mechanism.

claim: 5 dpf larvae exhibited repeatable, photo-activated motor responses to 2 s of exposure to light every 5 min.
source: 5 dpf larvae exhibited repeatable, photo-activated motor responses to 2 s of exposure to light every 5 min, whereas larvae treated with DMSO exhibited no such responses (Figure 7A–B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Treatment x Timebin Interaction: 38F2,44 = 6.36, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test with p<0.01) and reference to Figures 7A-B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 showing experimental data.

claim: Larvae treated with DMSO exhibited no photo-activated motor responses to 2 s of exposure to light every 5 min.
source: 5 dpf larvae exhibited repeatable, photo-activated motor responses to 2 s of exposure to light every 5 min, whereas larvae treated with DMSO exhibited no such responses (Figure 7A–B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Treatment x Timebin Interaction: 38F2,44 = 6.36, p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test with p<0.01) and reference to Figures 7A-B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1 showing experimental data.

claim: Light exposures significantly increased the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the pallium of larvae exposed to Optovin.
source: Twelve hours following the end of this session, light exposures significantly increased the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the pallium of larvae exposed to Optovin (Figure 7C; Drug x Light Treatment interaction; 39F1,32 = 4.47, p=0.04), whereas light treatments had no effect on the proportion of PCNA+ cells in DMSO-incubated larvae.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (F-test with p=0.04) and reference to Figure 7C showing experimental data.

claim: Light treatments had no effect on the proportion of PCNA+ cells in DMSO-incubated larvae.
source: Twelve hours following the end of this session, light exposures significantly increased the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the pallium of larvae exposed to Optovin (Figure 7C; Drug x Light Treatment interaction; 39F1,32 = 4.47, p=0.04), whereas light treatments had no effect on the proportion of PCNA+ cells in DMSO-incubated larvae.
evidence: The claim is supported by the statistical analysis and experimental design described in the text.

claim: 6 dpf larvae deficient in trunk DRGs did not exhibit the optovin-and-light-dependent increase in the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the pallium compared to controls.
source: Furthermore, 6 dpf larvae deficient in trunk DRGs (using a transient 8–30 hpf treatment with AG1478 as above) did not exhibit this optovin-and-light-dependent increase in the proportion of PCNA+ cells in the pallium compared to controls (8–30 hpf DMSO treatment; Figure 7D; 40t13 = 2.33, p=0.04).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (t-test with p=0.04) and reference to Figure 7D showing experimental data.

claim: The postembryonic brain exhibits experience-dependent development, in which sensory experience guides normal brain growth.
source: The postembryonic brain exhibits experience-dependent development, in which sensory experience guides normal brain growth.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract summarizing the broader context of the research.

claim: Neuroplasticity is thought to occur primarily through structural and functional changes in pre-existing neurons.
source: This neuroplasticity is thought to occur primarily through structural and functional changes in pre-existing neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about established scientific understanding.

claim: Movement maintains an expanded pool of forebrain neural precursors by promoting progenitor self-renewal over the production of neurons.
source: We found that movement maintains an expanded pool of forebrain neural precursors by promoting progenitor self-renewal over the production of neurons.
evidence: This is a summary claim in the abstract based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Physical cues associated with swimming (bodily movement) increase neurogenesis.
source: Physical cues associated with swimming (bodily movement) increase neurogenesis and these cues appear to be conveyed by dorsal root ganglia (DRG) in the zebrafish body: DRG-deficient larvae exhibit attenuated neurogenic responses to movement and targeted photoactivation of DRG in immobilized larvae expands the pallial pool of proliferative cells.
evidence: This is a summary claim in the abstract based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: DRG-deficient larvae exhibit attenuated neurogenic responses to movement.
source: Physical cues associated with swimming (bodily movement) increase neurogenesis and these cues appear to be conveyed by dorsal root ganglia (DRG) in the zebrafish body: DRG-deficient larvae exhibit attenuated neurogenic responses to movement and targeted photoactivation of DRG in immobilized larvae expands the pallial pool of proliferative cells.
evidence: This is a summary claim in the abstract based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Targeted photoactivation of DRG in immobilized larvae expands the pallial pool of proliferative cells.
source: Physical cues associated with swimming (bodily movement) increase neurogenesis and these cues appear to be conveyed by dorsal root ganglia (DRG) in the zebrafish body: DRG-deficient larvae exhibit attenuated neurogenic responses to movement and targeted photoactivation of DRG in immobilized larvae expands the pallial pool of proliferative cells.
evidence: This is a summary claim in the abstract based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: During postembryonic development, the brain begins processing sensory information from the environment for the first time and continues to grow, exhibiting elevated levels of neuroplasticity compared to later stages of life.
source: During postembryonic development, the brain begins processing sensory information from the environment for the first time and continues to grow, exhibiting elevated levels of neuroplasticity compared to later stages of life.
evidence: This is a statement about established scientific understanding of postembryonic brain development.

claim: The combination of sensory processing and continued growth makes postembryonic brain development highly susceptible to sensory experience.
source: The combination of these factors makes postembryonic brain development highly susceptible to sensory experience (Knudsen, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Knudsen, 2004.

claim: Neurogenesis persists postembryonically throughout the brain, either ceasing or curtailing in adolescence or adulthood.
source: However, neurogenesis persists postembryonically throughout the brain, either ceasing or curtailing in adolescence or adulthood (Lindsey and Tropepe, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lindsey and Tropepe, 2006.

claim: Some neuronal populations appear to be uniquely generated during postembryonic development.
source: Some neuronal populations appear to be uniquely generated during postembryonic development (Wei et al., 2011), and this process may be regulated by sensory experience (He et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wei et al., 2011.

claim: Postembryonic neurogenesis may be regulated by sensory experience.
source: Some neuronal populations appear to be uniquely generated during postembryonic development (Wei et al., 2011), and this process may be regulated by sensory experience (He et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to He et al., 2014.

claim: One of the best-characterized models of experience-dependent regulation of neurogenesis is the increase in cell proliferation in the subgranular zone (SGZ) of the dentate gyrus in the adult mammalian hippocampus (HP) following periods of aerobic running exercise.
source: Outside of postembryonic development, one of the best-characterized models of experience-dependent regulation of neurogenesis is the increase in cell proliferation in the subgranular zone (SGZ) of the dentate gyrus in the adult mammalian hippocampus (HP) following periods of aerobic running exercise (van Praag et al., 1999a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to van Praag et al., 1999a.

claim: Studies have linked exercise-induced neurogenesis to improvements in cognition, such as spatial learning.
source: Since its initial discovery, studies have gone on to link exercise-induced neurogenesis to improvements in cognition, such as spatial learning (van Praag et al., 1999b) and cognitive flexibility (Anacker and Hen, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to van Praag et al., 1999b.

claim: Studies have linked exercise-induced neurogenesis to improvements in cognitive flexibility.
source: Since its initial discovery, studies have gone on to link exercise-induced neurogenesis to improvements in cognition, such as spatial learning (van Praag et al., 1999b) and cognitive flexibility (Anacker and Hen, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Anacker and Hen, 2017.

claim: Studies have incorporated exercise as a therapeutic intervention to combat neuropsychiatric disorders associated with impaired neurogenesis.
source: Studies have also incorporated exercise as a therapeutic intervention to combat neuropsychiatric disorders associated with impaired neurogenesis (Vakhrusheva et al., 2016; Kandola et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vakhrusheva et al., 2016 and Kandola et al., 2016.

claim: There is a positive correlation between physical activity and cognitive function reported in human children.
source: Furthermore, such a relationship between movement and forebrain growth early in development may help explain the positive correlation between physical activity and cognitive function reported in human children (Tomporowski et al., 2008; Best, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tomporowski et al., 2008 and Best, 2010.

claim: Larval zebrafish first begin to exhibit voluntary movements during the developmental period studied.
source: Here, we sought to investigate the relationship between movement and neurogenesis in larval zebrafish during a developmental period in which they first begin to exhibit voluntary movements (Buss and Drapeau, 2001), have brains and peripheral nervous systems sufficiently developed to process sensory input, and continue to exhibit elevated rates of neurogenesis in many brain divisions compared to adulthood (Lindsey and Tropepe, 2006; Feliciano et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Buss and Drapeau, 2001.

claim: Larval zebrafish continue to exhibit elevated rates of neurogenesis in many brain divisions compared to adulthood.
source: Here, we sought to investigate the relationship between movement and neurogenesis in larval zebrafish during a developmental period in which they first begin to exhibit voluntary movements (Buss and Drapeau, 2001), have brains and peripheral nervous systems sufficiently developed to process sensory input, and continue to exhibit elevated rates of neurogenesis in many brain divisions compared to adulthood (Lindsey and Tropepe, 2006; Feliciano et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lindsey and Tropepe, 2006 and Feliciano et al., 2015.

claim: Dorsal root ganglia (DRG) are sensory neurons that convey mechanical sensations from the zebrafish trunk.
source: Finally, we tested whether dorsal root ganglia (DRG), sensory neurons that convey mechanical sensations from the zebrafish trunk, are required to mediate movement-dependent neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the known function of DRG.

claim: Movement restraint reduced swimming on 6 to 8 dpf both between groups.
source: Movement restraint reduced swimming on 6 to 8 dpf both between groups (B; control: n4,6,8 dpf = 12, 14, 11; restraint, n4,6,8 dpf = 13, 18, 18; Data are represented as mean ± SEM) and within individual larvae (C; control n = 6; restraint n = 13).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint reduced swimming on 6 to 8 dpf within individual larvae.
source: Movement restraint reduced swimming on 6 to 8 dpf both between groups (B; control: n4,6,8 dpf = 12, 14, 11; restraint, n4,6,8 dpf = 13, 18, 18; Data are represented as mean ± SEM) and within individual larvae (C; control n = 6; restraint n = 13).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C showing experimental data.

claim: Movement restraint reduced the proportion of fast swims (>10 mm/s) exhibited by larvae by 6–8 dpf.
source: Movement restraint also reduced the proportion of fast swims (>10 mm/s) exhibited by larvae by 6–8 dpf (D; n = 18).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1D showing experimental data.

claim: Treatment with AG1478 from 8 to 30 hpf prevented development of DRG along the trunk in larvae by 3 dpf without affecting RB neuron populations dorsal to the spinal cord.
source: Treatment with AG1478 from 8 to 30 hpf prevented development of DRG along the trunk in larvae by 3 dpf without affecting RB neuron populations dorsal to the spinal cord (Aii-iii).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6Aii-iii showing experimental data.

claim: Earlier treatment with AG1478 did not affect swimming compared to DMSO-treated controls on 8 dpf.
source: Earlier treatment with AG1478 did not affect swimming compared to DMSO-treated controls on 8 dpf (B; n = 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 6B showing experimental data.

claim: By 9 dpf, restrained larvae in both DMSO and AG1478 treatments exhibited fewer pallial PCNA+ cells compared to controls.
source: By 9 dpf, restrained larvae in both DMSO (F-G; control n = 6, restraint n = 7) and AG1478 (H-I; control n = 8, restraint n = 6) treatments exhibited fewer pallial PCNA+ cells compared to controls, however, AG1478-treated controls exhibited fewer pallial PCNA+ cells compared to DMSO-treated controls, despite similar swimming behaviour.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 6F-I showing experimental data.

claim: AG1478-treated controls exhibited fewer pallial PCNA+ cells compared to DMSO-treated controls, despite similar swimming behaviour.
source: By 9 dpf, restrained larvae in both DMSO (F-G; control n = 6, restraint n = 7) and AG1478 (H-I; control n = 8, restraint n = 6) treatments exhibited fewer pallial PCNA+ cells compared to controls, however, AG1478-treated controls exhibited fewer pallial PCNA+ cells compared to DMSO-treated controls, despite similar swimming behaviour.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figures 6F-I showing experimental data.

claim: Optovin is a small molecule that enables photoactivation of TRPA1 receptors.
source: We used an optopharmacological approach to activate DRGs by exposing larvae to a combination of light and Optovin, a small molecule that enables photoactivation of TRPA1 receptors (Kokel et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kokel et al., 2013.

claim: TRPA1 receptors are found in DRG, trigeminal neurons and Rohon-Beard cells in larval zebrafish.
source: TRPA1 receptors are found in DRG (Vandewauw et al., 2013), trigeminal neurons and Rohon-Beard cells in larval zebrafish (Prober et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vandewauw et al., 2013 and Prober et al., 2008.

claim: In zebrafish, Optovin acts specifically on the TRPA1b paralog, which is exclusively expressed in sensory ganglia up to 5 dpf.
source: In zebrafish, Optovin acts specifically on the TRPA1b paralog, which is exclusively expressed in sensory ganglia up to 5 dpf (Prober et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Prober et al., 2008.

claim: Movement-dependent regulation of postembryonic forebrain cell proliferation appears to occur predominantly through regulating self-renewal and the production of differentiated cells over factors that might affect the absolute number of cells produced, such as cell cycle length.
source: Because control and restrained larvae produced the same number of cells in the forebrain from 5 to 6 dpf, movement-dependent regulation of postembryonic forebrain cell proliferation appears to occur predominantly through regulating self-renewal and the production of differentiated cells over factors that might affect the absolute number of cells produced, such as cell cycle length.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the observation that control and restrained larvae produced the same number of cells.

claim: Movement-dependent maintenance of the progenitor pool may involve the Shh signaling pathway, which expands progenitor populations via symmetric cell division.
source: Within the neurogenic niche, movement-dependent maintenance of the progenitor pool may involve the Shh signaling pathway, which expands progenitor populations via symmetric cell division (Lai et al., 2003; Machold et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citations to Lai et al., 2003, Machold et al., 2003, and Yang et al., 2015.

claim: The lateral line is a system of hair cells distributed along the teleost body that detects changes in water flow.
source: One source of neural feedback that could detect physical movement is the lateral line, a system of hair cells distributed along the teleost body that detects changes in water flow (Dijkgraaf, 1963).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dijkgraaf, 1963.

claim: Copper sulfate is an ototoxin that ablates lateral line hair cells and impedes subsequent regeneration of these cells over the following days.
source: We treated 3 dpf larvae with 30 µM copper sulfate for 30 min, an ototoxin that ablates lateral line hair cells and impedes subsequent regeneration of these cells over the following days (Mackenzie and Raible, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mackenzie and Raible, 2012.

claim: In vertebrates, DRG collect sensory feedback from the body and communicate these signals via ascending pathways to the CNS in the spinal cord.
source: In vertebrates, DRG collect sensory feedback from the body and communicate these signals via ascending pathways to the CNS in the spinal cord (Vandewauw et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vandewauw et al., 2013.

claim: AG1478 treatment blocks the development of DRGs along the trunk, but does not affect DRG populations that are derived from neural crest cells in the head.
source: This continued modulation of neurogenesis in the older larvae may be attributed to the nature of our treatment, which blocks the development of DRGs along the trunk, but does not affect DRG populations that are derived from neural crest cells in the head that may also signal movement (Honjo et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Honjo et al., 2008.

claim: A previous study has demonstrated that treating zebrafish embryos with AG1478 can impair proliferation during embryogenesis in the zebrafish optic tectum.
source: A previous study has demonstrated that treating zebrafish embryos with AG1478 can impair proliferation during embryogenesis in the zebrafish optic tectum (Sato et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sato et al., 2015.

claim: Rohon-Beard cells were originally thought to die off entirely by 4 dpf.
source: Originally, RB cells were thought to die off entirely by 4 dpf (Reyes et al., 2004), but subsequent work using transgenic markers suggests they may persist up to 1–2 weeks post-fertilization (Kucenas et al., 2006; Palanca et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Reyes et al., 2004.

claim: Subsequent work using transgenic markers suggests Rohon-Beard cells may persist up to 1–2 weeks post-fertilization.
source: Originally, RB cells were thought to die off entirely by 4 dpf (Reyes et al., 2004), but subsequent work using transgenic markers suggests they may persist up to 1–2 weeks post-fertilization (Kucenas et al., 2006; Palanca et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kucenas et al., 2006 and Palanca et al., 2013.

claim: TRPA1 channels exhibit deep evolutionary conservation across vertebrates.
source: TRPA1 channels exhibit deep evolutionary conservation across vertebrates (Christensen and Corey, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Christensen and Corey, 2007.

claim: TRPA1 function has been implicated in touch stimuli in DRG of mice.
source: Whereas TRPA1 function has been implicated in touch stimuli in DRG of mice (Kwan et al., 2006; Brierley et al., 2011) and sensory neurons in C. elegans (Kindt et al., 2007), this channel is also associated with transducing chemosensory and nociceptive input (Prober et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kwan et al., 2006 and Brierley et al., 2011.

claim: TRPA1 function has been implicated in touch stimuli in sensory neurons in C. elegans.
source: Whereas TRPA1 function has been implicated in touch stimuli in DRG of mice (Kwan et al., 2006; Brierley et al., 2011) and sensory neurons in C. elegans (Kindt et al., 2007), this channel is also associated with transducing chemosensory and nociceptive input (Prober et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kindt et al., 2007.

claim: TRPA1 channel is associated with transducing chemosensory and nociceptive input.
source: Whereas TRPA1 function has been implicated in touch stimuli in DRG of mice (Kwan et al., 2006; Brierley et al., 2011) and sensory neurons in C. elegans (Kindt et al., 2007), this channel is also associated with transducing chemosensory and nociceptive input (Prober et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Prober et al., 2008.

claim: Motor development in most vertebrates begins early in the postembryonic period.
source: Motor development in most vertebrates begins early in the postembryonic period, including both viviparous species, such as with fetal motor development in humans (de Vries et al., 1982), and oviparous species, such as the larvae studied here.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Vries et al., 1982 for human fetal motor development.

claim: If the relationship between movement and neurogenesis is conserved across taxa, it may couple early motor and brain development.
source: Therefore, if conserved across taxa, this close relationship between movement and neurogenesis may couple early motor and brain development.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: There is a long-observed comorbidity of physical and mental impairments in children.
source: Furthermore, this relationship could help explain correlations between early physical and mental development, such as the long-observed comorbidity of physical and mental impairments (Barnett et al., 2012) and correlation between sedentary lifestyle and depression (Anton et al., 2006), which has been previously associated with impaired neurogenesis (Jacobs et al., 2000), in children.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Barnett et al., 2012.

claim: There is a correlation between sedentary lifestyle and depression in children.
source: Furthermore, this relationship could help explain correlations between early physical and mental development, such as the long-observed comorbidity of physical and mental impairments (Barnett et al., 2012) and correlation between sedentary lifestyle and depression (Anton et al., 2006), which has been previously associated with impaired neurogenesis (Jacobs et al., 2000), in children.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Anton et al., 2006.

claim: Depression has been previously associated with impaired neurogenesis.
source: Furthermore, this relationship could help explain correlations between early physical and mental development, such as the long-observed comorbidity of physical and mental impairments (Barnett et al., 2012) and correlation between sedentary lifestyle and depression (Anton et al., 2006), which has been previously associated with impaired neurogenesis (Jacobs et al., 2000), in children.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jacobs et al., 2000.
